MVVM keeps the screen separate from the decisions behind it. The View displays; the ViewModel offers screen-friendly properties and commands; the Model holds the underlying data and rules.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Open the Windows example

Open this project on Windows with .NET desktop development installed. MainWindow.xaml is the View. StudentViewModel.cs holds the ViewModel and a reusable command helper. App.xaml chooses the startup window. The window’s DataContext is the object the bindings read. The tiny code-behind only calls InitializeComponent.

Read a binding

<TextBox Text="{Binding Name, UpdateSourceTrigger=PropertyChanged}"/>
<Button Content="Add student" Command="{Binding AddCommand}"/>

Binding Name reads and writes the ViewModel’s Name property. PropertyChanged updates the source while typing. A command expresses an action without putting all business logic in a click handler. ObservableCollection tells the View when items are added or removed. Expected: Add remains disabled until a valid name and age are entered; after adding, a new list entry appears.

Keep layers understandable

Use services/repositories for database work rather than building SQL strings in XAML. The Model is not always an EF entity: it can be a domain object or DTO. MVVM and MVC solve related separation problems for different UI styles; their third parts have different jobs.

Try it yourself

Where should a “Can enrol?” rule live?

Worked answer

In a model/domain service, used by the ViewModel. Avoid burying reusable rules only in a UI control.

What happens if DataContext is missing?

Worked answer

Bindings may have no source. Inspect the Visual Studio Output window for binding errors; set the intended ViewModel.
